text: vitalBayes implements two-phase CW model blends standard declining-mortality trajectory senescence component. transition occurs user-defined age \(t_m\), typically set fraction age maturity (\(t_m = \frac{2}{3} t_{mat}\) default). \(t_m\), mortality follows standard CW model. \(t_m\), senescence function gradually increases mortality toward \(t_{max}\). Two senescence models available: Gompertz senescence (late_model = "gompertz"): \[M_{late}(t) = M_s \exp\!\left[r \cdot (t - t_{max})\right]\] \(M_s = c \cdot M(t_m)\) mortality plateau \(t_{max}\) (\(c\) = M_mult, default 2), \(r\) solved continuity \(t_m\): \[r = \frac{\ln\left(M(t_m) / M_s\right)}{t_m - t_{max}}\] produces accelerating increase mortality — modest first, pronounced organism approaches maximum age. pattern aligns actuarial models biological senescence hazard function increases exponentially (Gompertz, 1825). Logistic senescence (late_model = "logistic"): \[M_{late}(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \exp\!\left[-r \cdot (t - t_{max})\right]}\] \(K = 2 \, c \cdot M(t_m)\) \(r\) solved continuity \(t_m\). title: The Chen-Watanabe Reparameterization
text: transition early-phase CW model late-phase senescence model smoothed using logistic weighting function: \[w(t) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left[-\frac{2(t - t_m)}{s \cdot |t_{max} - t_m|}\right]}\] \(s\) smooth_factor (default \(\frac{1}{3}\)). blended mortality age : \[M(t) = (1 - w) \cdot M_{CW}(t) + w \cdot M_{late}(t)\] ensures smooth, differentiable transition rather sharp kink \(t_m\).

title: Growth Modeling with fit_bayesian_growth()
text: maturity-based parameterization derives \(k\) maturity milestones \((L_{mat}, t_{mat})\), ensuring growth curve passes maturity point prior information maturity models propagates growth posterior. derivation model-specific: substituting \(L(t_{mat}) = L_{mat}\) growth equation solving \(k\) yields: Von Bertalanffy: \[k_{VB} = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\!\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_0}{L_\infty - L_{mat}}\right)\] Gompertz: \[k_g = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\!\left(\frac{\ln(L_\infty / L_0)}{\ln(L_\infty / L_{mat})}\right)\] Logistic: \[k_l = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\!\left(\frac{L_{mat}(L_\infty - L_0)}{L_0(L_\infty - L_{mat})}\right)\] case, \(k\) deterministic function \((L_\infty, L_0, L_{mat}, t_{mat})\) — parameters either directly estimated Stan model informed upstream birth maturity fits. eliminates need specify prior \(k\) directly breaks \(L_\infty\)-\(k\) posterior correlation plagues traditional parameterizations. Note \(k\) different meanings across three models directly compared (e.g., Gompertz \(k_g\) generally larger VB \(k_{VB}\) species). matters biological inference resulting growth trajectory, numerical value \(k\). maturity-based? maturity-based parameterization offers several advantages. First, reduces posterior correlation: \((L_\infty, k)\) notoriously correlated traditional parameterization, replacing \(k\) \((L_{mat}, t_{mat})\) breaks collinearity. Second, provides observable anchoring: maturity milestones fall within observed data range, unlike \(L_\infty\) extrapolation beyond largest individuals. Third, prior information upstream maturity models propagates directly growth estimates, providing informative regularization sexes. Fourth, enforces biological coherence: fitted growth curve necessarily passes \((t_{mat}, L_{mat})\), real biological constraint rather mathematical convenience. full derivation, see model equations reference Stan source code.
code: # First, fit maturity models mat_data <- growth_data[embryo == FALSE & !is.na(mat)]  L50_fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity = "mat", lt = "fl", sex = "sex",   data = mat_data,   use_pooling = TRUE )  t50_fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity = "mat", age = "age", sex = "sex",   data = mat_data[!is.na(age)],   use_pooling = TRUE )  # Optional: fit birth model for L0 prior birth_fit <- fit_bayesian_birth(   embryo_lts = growth_data[embryo == TRUE, fl],   free_swimming_lts = growth_data[embryo == FALSE, fl] )  # Maturity-based growth model growth_mat <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt        = "fl",   age       = "age",   sex       = "sex",   data      = gdata,   model     = "v",   k_based   = FALSE,                    # Use maturity-based parameterization   length.mature_stanfit = L50_fit,       # Provides Lmat prior   age.mature_stanfit    = t50_fit,       # Provides tmat prior   birth_stanfit         = birth_fit,     # Provides L0 prior   parallel  = TRUE )  # k is now a derived quantity growth_mat$summary(c("Linf", "L0", "Lmat", "tmat", "k", "sigma"))

text: critical issue growth modeling: unconstrained \(L_\infty\) often converges values largest observed individuals — biologically impossible. vitalBayes enforces \(L_\infty > L_{max}\) (maximum observed length data), prior mean set Linf_multiplier \(\times\) \(L_{max}\) (default 1.05, .e., 5% maximum observed length). Note data argument can include incomplete cases (length without age), used determine \(L_{max}\). useful dataset contains measured individuals aged — lengths still inform plausible range \(L_\infty\).
code: # Lmax is auto-detected from data (including rows without age) growth_fit <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt   = "fl",   age  = "age",   data = gdata ) # Message: "Lmax from data: 98.5 cm"  # Or specify manually (e.g., if you have length data without age) growth_fit <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt   = "fl",   age  = "age",   data = gdata,   Lmax = c(100, 95)  # Female, Male )

title: Maturity Ogive Estimation with fit_bayesian_maturity()
text: \[P(\text{mature}_i) = \Phi[\beta \cdot (x_i - x_{50})]\] \(x\) either length (\(L\)) age (\(t\)), \(x_{50}\) value 50% individuals mature. Derived quantities: \(x_{05} = x_{50} - 1.645/\beta\) (5% maturity) \(x_{95} = x_{50} + 1.645/\beta\) (95% maturity) Transition width \(= x_{95} - x_{05} = 3.29/\beta\)

text: Elasmobranch datasets often imbalanced sex ratios. 150 females 34 males, male estimate wide credible intervals fit independently. Partial pooling addresses modeling sex-specific parameters draws common distribution: \[\log(L_{50,s}) = \mu + \tau \cdot \eta_s, \quad \eta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\] model learns appropriate degree pooling (\(\tau\)) data: Large \(\tau\) → sexes different → estimates stay separated Small \(\tau\) → sexes similar → estimates shrink together Sparse sex → borrows strength sex comprehensive treatment, see vignette("partial_pooling") Partial Pooling section Statistical Methods guide.

title: Age-Specific Natural Mortality with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Chen-Watanabe model derives age-specific mortality relationship body growth mortality risk von Bertalanffy dynamics. \(L_0\)-parameterized form used vitalBayes, model : \[M(t) = \frac{k_{VB} \cdot L_\infty}{L(t)}\] \(k_{VB}\) von Bertalanffy growth coefficient serving asymptotic mortality rate (\(M_\infty\)), \(L_\infty\) asymptotic length, \(L(t)\) predicted length age \(t\). Mortality inversely proportional body size: small, young individuals experience highest mortality, declines organism grows toward \(L_\infty\). equation involves \(k\) two distinct roles. \(k_{VB}\) numerator theoretical constant derived CW formulation von Bertalanffy assumptions — must always VB growth coefficient, regardless growth model actually fitted. \(L(t)\) denominator growth trajectory prediction — come whatever model best describes organism’s actual growth dynamics. Gompertz Logistic model fitted, vitalBayes uses native growth equation native \(k\) \(L(t)\), computing separate VB-equivalent \(k\) \(M_\infty\). VB-equivalent derived shared biological milestones \((L_\infty, L_0, L_{mat}, t_{mat})\): \[k_{VB}^{equiv} = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\!\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_0}{L_\infty - L_{mat}}\right)\] k-based fits without maturity milestones, derivative-matching fallback used (see Derivative-Based Conversion ). Chen-Watanabe model also supports two-phase extension late-life senescence, mortality transitions declining CW trajectory increasing senescence function (Gompertz Logistic) fraction age maturity. complete mathematical development CW reparameterization, normalized growth coefficient \(G(t)\), senescence extensions, see vignette("chen_watanabe_reparameterization").

title: Age-Specific Natural Mortality with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Peterson-Wroblewski model estimates mortality allometric relationship body weight mortality rate, derived empirical data pelagic fish populations: \[M(W) = 1.92 \cdot W(t)^{-0.25}\] \(W(t)\) body weight grams age \(t\), computed predicted length via user-supplied length-weight function \(W = f(L)\). \(-0.25\) exponent reflects metabolic scaling theory: metabolic rate scales approximately \(W^{0.75}\) (Kleiber’s law), mortality assumed proportional mass-specific metabolic rate, yielding \(W^{-0.25}\) dependence. Unlike CW model, PW model requires length-weight relationship function (provided via lw_fun argument). model operates predicted body weight rather growth model parameters directly, inherently growth-model-agnostic. growth model predicts \(L(t)\) can combined \(L\)-\(W\) conversion produce mortality estimates. length--age predictions use native growth model’s \(k\) (VB-equivalent), since PW model derived VB-specific assumptions.

title: Age-Specific Natural Mortality with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Lorenzen model relates natural mortality body size empirical calibration across broad taxonomic range. vitalBayes supports two formulations. Weight-based (Lorenzen, 1996): \[M(W) = \alpha \cdot W(t)^{\beta}\] \(\alpha\) \(\beta\) allometric parameters estimated meta-analysis marine freshwater fishes (\(\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(3.69, \, 0.502)\), \(\beta \sim \mathcal{N}(-0.305, \, 0.029)\)). Like PW model, purely weight-based: \(k\) appear mortality equation serves predict \(L(t)\) via native growth model. native \(k\) native growth equation always used. Growth-based (Lorenzen, 2022): \[\ln M = 0.28 - 1.30 \, \ln\!\left(\frac{L(t)}{L_\infty}\right) + 1.08 \, \ln(k_{VB})\] formulation dual-\(k\) structure Chen-Watanabe. \(\ln(k_{VB})\) term calibrated von Bertalanffy parameters (Lorenzen, 2022), must VB growth coefficient. \(L(t)/L_\infty\) ratio represents relative body size age use native growth trajectory accurate prediction. inputs come Gompertz Logistic fit, vitalBayes passes native \(k\) \(L(t)\) prediction separate \(k_{VB}^{equiv}\) regression term. growth-based formulation advantage requiring length-weight relationship, making useful \(L\)-\(W\) data unavailable.

Survival probability (M_target = NULL, p = ...): Specify proportion cohort expected survive maximum age \(t_{max}\). target cumulative hazard : \[H_{target} = -\ln(p)\] common choice \(p = 0.001\) (0.1% survival \(t_{max}\)), produces moderate scaling long-lived species. directly interpretable target: scaled schedule produce exactly \(S(t_{max}) = p\) cumulative hazard framework. Empirical relationship (M_target = function(tmax) ...): Supply function \(t_{max}\), et al. (2015) estimator: \[\bar{M}_{target} = 4.899 \cdot t_{max}^{-0.916}\] interpreted average mortality rate lifespan, producing \(H_{target} = \bar{M}_{target} \times t_{max}\). Fixed value (M_target = 0.15): Directly specify target mean mortality literature estimates independent analyses, also interpreted lifespan-averaged rate (\(H_{target} = 0.15 \times t_{max}\)).

title: Cohort Survival Simulation with simulate_survivorship()
text: Cumulative survival age \(t\) given age-specific mortality schedule \(M()\) : \[S(t) = \exp\left(-\int_0^t M() \, da\right)\] function evaluates integral numerically via trapezoidal quadrature.

code: Birth  ──▶  Maturity  ──▶  Growth  ──▶  Mortality/Survival (L₀)       (L₅₀, t₅₀)    (L∞, k)         (M, S(t)) library(vitalBayes) library(data.table)  data(growth_data)  # Stage 1: Birth size ───────────────────────────────────────── birth_fit <- fit_bayesian_birth(   embryo_lts        = growth_data[embryo == TRUE, fl],   free_swimming_lts = growth_data[embryo == FALSE, fl] )  # Stage 2: Maturity ─────────────────────────────────────────── mat_data <- growth_data[embryo == FALSE & !is.na(mat)]  L50_fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity = "mat", lt = "fl", sex = "sex",   data = mat_data, use_pooling = TRUE )  t50_fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity = "mat", age = "age", sex = "sex",   data = mat_data[!is.na(age)], use_pooling = TRUE )  # Stage 3: Growth ───────────────────────────────────────────── growth_fit <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt = "fl", age = "age", sex = "sex",   data = growth_data[embryo == FALSE & !is.na(age)],   model   = "vb",   k_based = FALSE,      # Maturity-based parameterization   birth_stanfit         = birth_fit,   length.mature_stanfit = L50_fit,   age.mature_stanfit    = t50_fit,   use_pooling = TRUE )  # Stage 4: Mortality & Survival ─────────────────────────────── mort <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method       = "CW",   Linf = c(100, 8), L0 = c(30, 3), Lmat = c(70, 5), tmat = c(12, 2),   growth_model = "vb",   iter = 2000, scaled = TRUE, p = 0.001 )  surv <- simulate_survivorship(mc_object = mort, n = 50000, n_iter = 2000) surv$Aggregate$Age_of_Death surv$Aggregate$Survival_to_tmat

title: Chen-Watanabe Natural Mortality (\(L_0\) Parameterization) — M_chen_watanabe_L0
text: standard Chen-Watanabe formulation expresses mortality : $$M(t) = \frac{k}{1 - e^{-k(t - t_0)}}$$ \(t_0\) theoretical age length zero — parameter direct biological interpretation can take implausible values, particularly growth data sparse. reparameterize using relationship \(t_0\) \(L_0\) (birth length) von Bertalanffy dynamics: $$L_0 = L_\infty(1 - e^{kt_0})$$ algebraic manipulation (see vignette), \(L_0\)-parameterized form becomes: $$M(t) = \frac{k_{VB} \cdot L_\infty}{L(t)}$$ \(k_{VB}\) von Bertalanffy growth coefficient (VB-equivalent non-VB fits) \(L(t)\) predicted length age \(t\) native growth model.

title: Lorenzen Natural Mortality Model — M_lorenzen
text: Two formulations available: Weight-based (Lorenzen 1996): $$M(W) = \alpha \cdot W^{\beta}$$ \(\alpha \sim N(3.69, 0.502)\) \(\beta \sim N(-0.305, 0.029)\). Body weight \(W(t)\) computed predicted length via user-supplied length-weight function using native growth model trajectory. Growth-based (Lorenzen 2022): $$\ln M = 0.28 - 1.30 \ln(L(t)/L_\infty) + 1.08 \ln(k_{VB})$$ formulation calibrated using von Bertalanffy parameters. \(L(t)/L_\infty\) ratio computed native growth model accurate relative-size estimates, \(k_{VB}\) must VB-equivalent growth coefficient (native VB \(k\)) regression coefficients calibrated VB parameters.

title: Compute Von Bertalanffy-Equivalent Growth Coefficient — compute_k_vb_equivalent
text: key insight three growth models use different functional forms produce different numerical \(k\) values, estimate underlying biological quantities: asymptotic length, birth size, maturity milestones. VB-equivalent \(k\) computed : $$k_{VB}^{equiv} = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_0}{L_\infty - L_{mat}}\right)$$ growth coefficient produce von Bertalanffy curve passing biological milestones \((0, L_0)\) \((t_{mat}, L_{mat})\) asymptote \(L_\infty\). input growth fit von Bertalanffy maturity-based parameterization, computation exactly reproduces fitted \(k\). input Gompertz Logistic, produces VB-equivalent \(k\) encodes biological growth information. von Bertalanffy model tends produce unstable \(L_\infty\) estimates data sparse older ages - common situation elasmobranch research. Gompertz Logistic models often provide reliable fits cases. deriving VB-equivalent \(k\) biological milestones, users can select growth model best fits data still using Chen-Watanabe mortality estimation maintaining theoretical coherence (since CW derived VB assumptions).

Can numeric scalar (fixed target), function tmax (e.g., function(tmax) 4.899 * tmax^(-0.916) et al. 2015), NULL derive survival probability p. tmax Maximum age (required M_target function NULL). p Probability surviving tmax. title: Scale Mortality Schedule to Target via Cumulative Hazard — scale_mortality
text: scaling finds proportional constant \(c\) : $$M_{scaled}(t) = c \times M_{raw}(t)$$ constant \(c\) determined matching cumulative hazard target. cumulative hazard computed via trapezoidal integration: $$H_{raw} = \int_0^{t_{max}} M_{raw}() \, da \approx \sum_i   \frac{\Delta a_i}{2} \left[ M(a_i) + M(a_{+1}) \right]$$ survival-probability target (M_target = NULL): $$c = \frac{-\ln(p)}{H_{raw}}$$ ensures \(S(t_{max}) = \exp\!\left(-c \cdot H_{raw}\right) = p\) exactly. fixed mean-mortality target (numeric function tmax): $$c = \frac{\bar{M}_{target} \times t_{max}}{H_{raw}}$$ interprets target average mortality lifespan, cumulative hazard scaled schedule equals \(\bar{M}_{target} \times t_{max}\). approach preferred arithmetic-mean-based scaling directly constrains biologically relevant quantity (cumulative survival) rather proxy, invariant age grid spacing.
